a:r.a:t: Degradation Intermediates of Tryptophan Are to Synthesize Other Molecules

p:cNvPr.descr: An image depicting tryptophan as a precursor. On the top left is tryptophan, which is a hexagon with a pentagon to the right. They share a double-bonded side. Each side of the hexagon is double-bonded. The top point is H over C. The top left point is HC. The bottom left point is HC (all Cs are pink). The bottom point is CH. The top right and bottom points are both C (in pink). The pentagon also shares those Cs. The bottom right point is N over H (N is pink). The top right side is double-bonded. The top right point is a blue C, which bonds up to CH2, which bonds right to CH, which bonds up to NH3 (plus sign over N), and right to COO-. To the right of the this is an arrow pointing right to nicotinate (niacin), a precursor of NAD and NADP. This is a pentagon with double-bonded sides on the left, top right, and bottom right. Beginning at the top, clockwise, the points are H over C, C, CH, N, HC, and HC. All Cs are pink. The top right C bonds right to COO- (C is blue). Tryptophan also has an arrow pointing down and right to indoleacetate, a plant growth factor. It has a hexagon on the left sharing a side with a pentagon on the right. This shared side is double-bonded. The hexagon has alternating double-bonded sides, and the pentagon’s top right side is double-bonded. The bottom right point of the pentagon is N over H, and the top point bonds up to CH2COO-. Tryptophan also has an arrow pointing down to serotonin, a neurotransmitter. This is a replica of indoleacetate, but the top left point of the hexagon bonds up and left to HO. The top point of the pentagon bonds up to CH2CH2NH3 (plus sign over N).
